extracted.intended_audience: mathematics students, educators, and enthusiasts (undergraduate and general-interest mathematicians)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and reflective criteria for judging or composing a 'beautiful' mathematical proof, focusing on experiential, stylistic, and structural qualities rather than formal correctness alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: The proof uses few assumptions or previous results and comes together swiftly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simplicity often makes a solution feel almost obvious and can 'untangle' a knotted problem by breaking it into simpler claims. However, too much speed or compression can feel abrupt and harm pacing (the author notes Proof (1) felt fast and abrupt).

rubrics_metrics.name: Concision
rubrics_metrics.description: The proof is surprisingly succinct; every part is effective and necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concision means no wasted steps — the argument is tight and economically expressed. The post praises proofs that occupy little space yet leave the reader satisfied; conversely excessive length without clear payoff is undesirable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpectedness
rubrics_metrics.description: The proof derives a result in an unexpected or surprising way, often using an unrelated area of mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unexpected methods can delight by connecting disparate areas and producing surprising viewpoints. The write-up highlights proofs that use creative, non-obvious approaches as especially pleasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality
rubrics_metrics.description: The proof is based on an original or not-before-seen insight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original insights (creative set-ups or novel constructions) make a proof feel lovely — e.g., Proof (7) is described as a 'lovely proof' with a creative, simple set-up and clear steps. Originality overlaps with unexpectedness but emphasizes novelty of idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalisability
rubrics_metrics.description: The proof can be easily extended to a larger family of similar problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs that generalize often gain retrospective praise because they reveal broader structure and have far‑reaching ramifications beyond the specific statement proved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation / Readability (Narrative Quality)
rubrics_metrics.description: A beautifully written proof should read like a story with grammar, punctuation, a beginning, middle and end; signposting is important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good presentation includes clear signposting (especially in constructive proofs), coherent structure, and readable exposition. The author notes that presentation affects the emotional experience: sometimes withholding signposts leads to a satisfying discovery, but often signposting helps the reader follow the construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insightfulness / Explanatory Power
rubrics_metrics.description: The proof unveils connections, relationships, or structure previously hidden and gives understanding, not just verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proof that 'moulds the shape' of a problem or 'reveals a familiar, satisfying shape' is valued for the explanatory joy it gives (quoting Thurston on the joy of explanations). This criterion emphasizes understanding and conceptual illumination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pacing and Flow
rubrics_metrics.description: The tempo of the argument — neither too abrupt nor so prolonged that it distances the reader from the original problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speedy proofs can feel abrupt (Proof (1) example), very long set-ups can distance the reader, but a long proof that 'comes together swiftly and neatly' at the end can still feel satisfying (Proof (11) example). Appropriate pacing helps maintain engagement and connection to the problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retention of Problem Context and Visuals
rubrics_metrics.description: The proof keeps the original problem visually or conceptually present so the reader stays connected to what is being solved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintaining visuals or reminders of the original problem helps even longer proofs feel grounded; the author notes Proof (11) succeeds because visuals are retained, keeping the problem at the forefront of the reader's mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-patterns: Laborious Calculation and Heavy Reliance on Many Results
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs which involve long, laborious calculations or rely heavily on many previous results may be described as 'ugly' or 'clumsy'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post explicitly classifies such arguments as unattractive; they may prove the theorem but fail to provide the elegance, insight, or narrative satisfaction that constitute beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjectivity of Beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty in proofs is subjective; different readers value different combinations of the above criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author emphasizes that while the five elements (simplicity, concision, unexpectedness, originality, generalisability) are important, appreciation of beauty is personal (quoting Erdös: 'If you don't see why, someone can't tell you'). This warns against rigid scoring and acknowledges individual variation in tastes.
